meta.description: Yes, it is Shakespeare — Richard III, Act 1, scene 1, first printed 1597. But the sentence continues, and the winter is the part that has just ended.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Now is the winter of our discontent'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Shakespeare: the opening line of Richard III, printed 1597 and 1623. The full sentence says the opposite of what the quote implies.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: c. 1564 – 1616 · English playwright, poet and actor
answer.sourceLine: It is the opening line of The Tragedy of King Richard the Third, spoken by Richard, Duke of Gloucester — and it is genuine: the wording appears in the 1597 first quarto and again in the 1623 First Folio. The catch is that the sentence does not end there. It runs on into “Made glorious summer by this son of York,” which reverses the gloom almost everyone hears in the first line alone.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Tragedy of King Richard the Third
Act 1, scene 1, lines 1–2 — opening soliloquy of Richard, Duke of Gloucester
First quarto, London: Valentine Sims for Andrew Wise, 1597; again in the First Folio, 1623
Folger Shakespeare Library edition (based on the 1623 First Folio)

source.excerpt:
Now is the winter of our discontent
Made glorious summer by this son of York,
And all the clouds that loured upon our house
In the deep bosom of the ocean buried.
Now are our brows bound with victorious wreaths,
Our bruisèd arms hung up for monuments,
Our stern alarums changed to merry meetings,
Our dreadful marches to delightful measures.
trail: The play was written c. 1592–1594 and entered in the Stationers’ Register on 20 October 1597 by the bookseller Andrew Wise, who published the first quarto later that year; the Folio version followed in 1623 ↗.
The 1597 first quarto opens: “NOw is the winter of our discontent, / Made glorious summer by this sonne of Yorke:” — see the Internet Shakespeare Editions old-spelling transcription ↗.

The 1623 First Folio prints: “NOw is the Winter of our Discontent, / Made glorious Summer by this Son of Yorke:” — Folio 1 transcription ↗. The line has therefore been in print, in this wording, for more than four centuries.

Modern editors split on the second line. The Folger edition is based on the First Folio ↗ and keeps “son of York”; the more familiar “sun of York” is an editorial choice that makes the heraldic pun explicit.
source.excerptNote: Text as printed in the Folger Shakespeare edition ↗, which follows the First Folio and reads “son of York.” Many widely circulated modern texts, such as Open Source Shakespeare ↗, print “sun of York” instead.

author.bio: William Shakespeare (c. 23 April 1564 – 23 April 1616) was an English playwright, poet and actor, baptised at Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564. Richard III, written around 1592–1594, is one of his early history plays, and its opening soliloquy is among the most quoted passages in English — and among the most frequently quoted against its own meaning. He is also the single biggest magnet for invented quotations online, which makes the genuinely sourced lines worth pinning down precisely.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this quote
misattribution.intro: Nobody doubts the author. What gets misattributed here is the meaning — and, on quotation sites, the second line’s spelling.

items.who: Almost everyone who quotes the first line alone
items.why: Standing by itself the line sounds like a lament, as though we are in the thick of the misery. Shakespeare’s sentence says the opposite: Richard is reporting that the period of misery has been made into a glorious happy summer by the House of York’s victory — as set out in this reading of the speech ↗.

items.who: Quotation sites and many modern editions
items.why: The familiar “made glorious summer by this sun of York” is a modernisation. The 1597 quarto sets “this sonne of Yorke” ↗ and the 1623 Folio “this Son of Yorke.” Both spellings existed in period printing and the two words were homophones, so the copy does not settle the reading: Edward IV was literally the eldest surviving son of Richard, 3rd Duke of York ↗, and the Yorkist badge was a sun in splendour ↗. The pun runs on the homophone plus the badge, not on a failure of spelling.
Steinbeck’s last completed novel, The Winter of Our Discontent (1961), is sometimes assumed to have coined the phrase. Its title comes from the first two lines of Richard III ↗.

The name given to the UK strike wave of late September 1978 to February 1979 was taken from this opening line ↗, and is usually credited to Sun editor Larry Lamb — though the same source notes earlier use in a 1978 Downing Street note.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Shakespeare’s, and they have been in print since 1597 ↗. Only the sentence’s direction has been lost: the winter is the part that has just ended.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: Richard III opens with a man walking on alone and telling the audience, more or less, that everything is fine now. The Yorkists have won, his brother Edward sits on the throne, and the long miserable war is over — that is what “the winter of our discontent / Made glorious summer” is actually reporting. The joke, and the engine of the whole play, is that Richard finds peace unbearable and spends the rest of the speech deciding to wreck it.

So the line has spent more than four centuries being deployed to mean its opposite. Steinbeck borrowed it for a book jacket in 1961, British politics turned it into the label for a strike wave, and news writers still reach for it whenever things look bleak. A Royal Holloway Shakespearean has argued that the misuse costs us the sharper warning in the play ↗ — about a ruler who manufactures chaos because calm leaves him nothing to do.
detailsBody: Editions agree on the first line and part company on the second. The 1597 quarto sets “this sonne of Yorke” and the 1623 Folio “this Son of Yorke.” Editors who print “sun” are making the heraldic reading explicit; editors who print “son” are following the copy, since Edward was literally a son of the Duke of York.

Both readings are live at once, which is rather the point: Wikipedia prints the line as “this sun [or son] of York” ↗ and leaves the choice open, while Wikiquote simply prints the modernised “sun of York” ↗ with no note either way. Nothing about the first line — the part people actually quote — is in doubt.
